newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: Pledges come "thick and fast" for Iran -- Red Cross.
newsitem.headline: Pledges come "thick and fast" for Iran -- Red Cross.

text.p: Pledges have been coming in "thick and fast" in response to an appeal to help victims of Iran's massive earthquake, the International Federation of Red Cross and Red Crescent Societies said on Tuesday.
A spokeswoman for the Federation, which groups 171 national Red Cross and Red Crescent member societies, welcomed news that Iran had lowered its numbers for casualties of Saturday's quake.

A senior Interior Ministry official in Qaen, near the epicentre in the eastern region, said 1,560 people had been killed and 2,810 injured. No explanation was given for previous official reports that about 2,400 had died and 6,000 were injured.
"We are very pleased if the tragic numbers are down," Federation spokeswoman Marie-Francoise Borel told Reuters. "It had been difficult to get exact numbers."
"Shelter items are the priority now. Tents and blankets are needed, as well as water tanks," she added.
In a 24-hour period, the Federation raised seven million Swiss francs ($4.6 million) toward its 12 million swiss franc ($8.2 million) appeal issued on Monday.

The money was raised from four governments -- Britain, Denmark, Netherlands and Norway -- and from thirteen national Red Cross or Red Crescent societies in Austria, Belgium, Britain, Canada, Denmark, the Netherlands, Germany, Kuwait, Japan, Libya, Norway, Sweden and Switzerland. The EU's humanitarian agency ECHO also contributed.
But five million swiss francs ($3.3 million) more is badly needed in Iran, where 100,000 were left homeless and many villages lack clean drinking water, the Geneva-based body said.

"The pledges have been coming in thick and fast all day -- we are struggling to remember when there has been such a rapid and generous reaction over a 24-hour period to an appeal for a natural disaster," said Margareta Wahlstroem, under-secretary general for disaster response, said in an overnight statement.
"The magnitude of the disaster is growing by the hour and we expect the number of people needing our help to rise," Walhstroem added. "An immense task lies ahead."

The funds are being used to provide vital relief supplies -- including emergency food, shelter, clothing, cooking utensils water and hygiene items -- for at least 60,000 people over the next four months.
Relief goods have been flown into the airport at Meshat, north of the affected zone, according to Borel. They are then being taken by truck or helicopter to the area for distribution.
The Iranian Red Crescent has been working around the clock, deploying 4,300 rescue workers within hours of the quake, according to the Federation.
"It has distributed all emergency food stocks and relief items. Its warehouses are now empty," the Federation said.
Meanwhile United Nations agencies have pledged $360,000 to Iran's victims, the world body announced in New York on Monday.

The U.N. Department of Humanitarian Affairs (DHA), which has provided an emergency grant of $50,000 to purchase relief supplies locally, said it was sending a two-member disaster assessment and coordination team to Iran on Tuesday.

"In cooperation with the World Health Organisation, DHA is preparing an airlift of requested emergency relief items and medical supplies from the DHA warehouse in Pisa, Italy, subject to the approval of specific contents by the Iranian government," DHA said in a statement issued in Geneva.
Plastic water containers, cookers, lamps, power generators, shoes and clothing, canned food, blankets and medicine were needed on an emergency basis, according to the DHA statement.
